title: The sorrowful mysteries
hook: the agony, the scourging, the thorns, the carrying, the cross (Tuesdays and Fridays)
carry: walk the hard road with him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the luminous mysteries: the baptism, Cana, the kingdom, the Transfiguration, the Last Supper. Your line was the light years. Which of the five stayed with you? Day one hundred twenty-one.

Think of the worst week someone you love has had. A diagnosis. A funeral. A night in a hospital corridor with bad coffee. Now think of how you sat with them. You probably didn't fix anything. You just stayed. You walked next to them for a while. On Tuesdays and Fridays, Catholics who pray the rosary do something like that with Jesus. They take the beads and walk through the worst night and day of his life, one decade at a time. Five scenes, none of them easy. Today, the sorrowful mysteries.
screen: `THE WORST WEEK YOU'VE SEEN.` → `YOU DIDN'T FIX IT. YOU STAYED.` → `TUESDAYS AND FRIDAYS.`

segments.voice: Here are the five. First, the agony in the garden. The night before he dies, Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and Luke says his sweat fell like drops of blood. In the Douay-Rheims Bible his prayer is this: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Second, the scourging at the pillar: the Roman soldiers whip him. Third, the crowning with thorns: they twist a crown out of thorns, throw a purple cloak on him, and mock him as a king. Fourth, the carrying of the cross, through the streets, with a stranger named Simon of Cyrene pressed into helping. Fifth, the crucifixion: three hours on the cross, and death. Notice the word agony. In Luke's Greek it's agonia, and it first meant a contest, the strain of an athlete in a race. It's a struggle, not only pain. Why would anyone choose to pray through this, twice a week? Catholics give a few answers. One: love stays. Mary stood by the cross, and praying these mysteries is a way of standing there too. Two: the sorrowful mysteries are for people who are suffering. Someone in chemo, someone grieving, someone in prison can find their own night in his. Many Catholics offer a sorrowful decade for a particular person who is hurting. Three: they don't end here. The rosary never leaves him in the tomb. Tomorrow comes the glory. And one practical note: in his 2002 letter on the rosary, Pope John Paul the Second suggested the sorrowful mysteries for Tuesdays and Fridays, and many also pray them on the Sundays of Lent.
screen: `THE GARDEN, THE WHIP, THE THORNS.` · `THE CROSS CARRIED, THE CROSS.` · `AGONIA: A STRUGGLE, NOT ONLY PAIN.` · `A DECADE FOR SOMEONE WHO HURTS.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one sorrowful decade for someone suffering. Settle, and breathe. Pick one of the five scenes. The garden is a good one to start with. Picture it: night, olive trees, friends asleep. Now bring to mind one person who is in a hard place right now. Hold them there, in that garden, with him. If you pray the rosary, you can pray the decade for them, ten Hail Marys on the beads or your fingers. If you don't, just keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
The sorrowful mysteries. The garden, the pillar, the thorns, the cross carried, the cross. Five hard scenes, prayed so no one suffers alone. Today's word.
Your line: walk the hard road with him. Today, send one message to someone who's having a hard time. No advice. Just: I'm thinking of you. Day one hundred twenty-one.

original.note: Greek, Luke 22:44: a contest or struggle, the strain of a runner. English agony comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: five sad scenes to feel bad about.
what it means: five hard scenes Catholics walk through with Jesus, often for someone who is suffering, knowing the glory comes next.
what a scholar hears: agonia in Luke 22:44 is an athlete's word for struggle, and some early manuscripts of Luke leave out the verses about the bloody sweat.

notes: Days: Rosarium Virginis Mariae 38 suggests sorrowful mysteries on Tuesday and Friday; the Sundays of Lent custom is common practice. Confirm phrasing.
Luke 22:43–44 (angel, bloody sweat) is absent from some early manuscripts; mentioned only in the trapdoor. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this scholarly note.
Purple cloak (Mark 15:17; Matthew has scarlet): 'purple' used. Confirm.
Mary at the cross: John 19:25. Offering a decade for a person is common devotion, not a rule.
'ten Hail Marys on the beads or your fingers' — a decade also includes an Our Father and a Glory Be; simplified. Confirm.
